motivational.video_read: A ~3-hour English podcast where Raj Shamani interviews cognitive neuroscientist Dr. Sahar Yousef about attention, phones, habits, sleep and burnout. Most of the video is excellent but advisory (science aimed at productivity), which belongs to other finders. The material of my kind lives in the belief and reframe passages — the billionaire's brain, 'brains look for data that confirms your beliefs', 'be bored', the powerless-to-powerful confession — and in the moment where she dares the scrolling viewer directly.

near_misses.why_not: The 60-second eyes-closed replacement habit is a beautiful small instruction, but on the page it needs the whole whiteboard loop before it to mean anything.
'Stress doesn't kill. Never completing the stress cycle kills' is a genuine mic-drop, but the build (morning phone scroll) makes it long and it heals more than it fires up.
The 9-week detox results ('significantly less lonely, attention spans went up') is earned reassurance — you can undo it — but it is data-first and belongs partly to the science finder.
'If you want off days, go get a job' is a sharp hustle line, but the surrounding stretch slides into the manipulation riff, which ends on a directionless note.
'I am God. I create everything in my life' is spiritual with real conviction, but risks reading as out-there without the addiction backstory before it.

emotional.video_read: A three-hour Raj Shamani podcast with a cognitive neuroscientist about attention, phones, habits, sleep and burnout. Almost the entire video is instruction and science — territory that belongs to the general and motivation finders. The material of my kind lives in two places: her answer about why scrolling never satisfies loneliness, and the closing personal questions where she admits what her ambition cost her and how addiction humbled an expert.

near_misses.why_not: 'Try to remember three reels ago' breaks the fourth wall at the scrolling viewer — clever and true, but it lands as wit, not stillness.
'I even studied addiction and I still became addicted' — same confession as clip 3, but stated flatter here; the fuller version later is the one to take.
The morning-scroll roller coaster ending on 'never completing the stress cycle kills' — punchy, but it informs and instructs more than it holds; motivation/general territory.
'I am God, I create everything in my life' — the powerlessness-to-power reframe reads as self-help affirmation; the humbling half of the same answer (clip 3) is where the real feeling is.

entertainment.video_read: A ~3-hour Raj Shamani podcast with cognitive neuroscientist Dr. Sahar Yousef about attention, phones, sleep and habits. It is almost entirely polished teaching with very little interpersonal friction, so the entertainment value lives in a handful of scattered provocations, burns and direct-address gotchas rather than in any extended exchange. The coldest, most quotable moments sit in the second and third hours.

near_misses.why_not: The live multitasking test genuinely lands (17.72 to 41.35, 'more than double', mistakes admitted) but the full ladder with both writing silences runs well past the 2.5-minute discard line.
'That means you're dumber' is a gasp line, but the three-scenario study setup is long and the content is research explanation, not friction — the education finder's clip.
Confident multitaskers testing worse is a real irony ('It's like a joke. It's like science jokes') but reads flat without the live test around it.
'The world's gonna go on whether you're looking at it or not. You're not that important' is a good cold burn at news-addicted CEOs, a notch below the ones taken.
Raj's unplanned confession that he plays the victim card about his own sleep is genuine but soft, with no reaction beat to carry it.

general.video_read: A three-hour Raj Shamani podcast with cognitive neuroscientist Dr. Sahar Yousef about attention, phones, habits, sleep and burnout. The strongest material is concentrated in her mechanism explanations backed by named studies and live demonstrations — the phone-on-the-table study, the stress-cycle argument, the 9-week digital detox results — plus a few raw personal moments near the end. It is dense with clip-worthy stretches; the difficulty was cutting down, not finding.

near_misses.why_not: 'Brick wall to the average person, that person sees a door' is a great line, but the belief framing around it leans motivational-generic compared to the mechanism clips above.
The multitasking paper test is excellent, but the two live writing gaps push it past the five-minute discard line; the 'one 100' and Stanford clips carry the same idea tighter.
Shower-thought mechanism is genuinely useful, but it repeats the DMN/boredom material already covered by the 'be bored' clip.
The 3M break framework is saveable, but it arrives as a list and 'complete psychological detachment' is the only part with real depth.
The cognitive pause is a good tactic but thin on its own; the craving-loop clip covers the same ground with more force.
